lead: A sensor output is a number, and a number means nothing until two people agree what it counts. Units give that agreement; standards give a physical reference; calibration connects the two. Without this chain a pressure reading of 1.98 is just a voltage. This chapter builds the chain from the seven SI base units to the instrument on a plant floor, defines traceability, separates calibration from verification and adjustment, and ends with the static calibration procedure and its certificate.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 on what the sensor is converting, so that the input unit and the output unit are both clear before you compare them.

blocks.text: A sensor turns a physical quantity into a number. The number stays useless until everyone agrees on the size of the unit. The SI system fixes seven base units: the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time, the ampere (A) for current, the kelvin (K) for thermodynamic temperature, the mole (mol) for amount of substance, and the candela (cd) for luminous intensity.

Every other unit on a datasheet is built from these. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²; 1 Pa = 1 N/m²; 1 V = 1 kg·m²/(s³·A); 1 Ω = 1 V/A; 1 F = 1 C/V; 1 Hz = 1/s. The degree Celsius is a shifted kelvin: t(°C) = T(K) − 273.15, so a temperature difference of 1 °C equals 1 K, but 20 °C is 293.15 K, not 20 K.

Two habits catch most errors. Write the unit beside every number. Run a dimensional check: sensitivity = output unit ÷ input unit. A pressure sensor giving 19.9 mV/kPa has the dimensions of voltage per pressure (V/Pa); the numerical value changes with the unit, the dimension does not. To convert 0.137 V/psi to V/kPa, divide by 6.89476 kPa/psi: S = 0.137 V/psi ÷ 6.89476 kPa/psi = 0.0199 V/kPa = 19.9 mV/kPa. To go the other way (mV/kPa → mV/psi), multiply by 6.89476. Rule: multiply by the ratio that cancels the old unit, and check direction: 1 psi is bigger than 1 kPa, so a sensitivity per psi is a bigger number than per kPa.

sections.h3: The ladder of standards and traceability

blocks.text: You cannot check a volt against nature on a shop floor. So the world uses a ladder, and every rung is calibrated against the rung above it.

items: International: the BIPM, near Paris, coordinates the SI and key comparisons between national institutes.
National primary: in India, CSIR–National Physical Laboratory, New Delhi, maintains the national standards and realises the SI units.
Secondary: held by calibration laboratories and calibrated against the national standard. Some syllabi call this the reference standard; both names mean the same rung.
Working: the dead-weight tester, standard resistor or calibrator in the plant instrument room, checked against a secondary standard.

blocks.text: Each rung is more accurate than the one below, typically by a factor of four to ten. A standard only as good as the device under test proves nothing.

Traceability is what makes the ladder usable: an unbroken chain of calibrations, each link with a stated uncertainty, each documented, ending at a primary standard. A sensor is traceable when you can show that chain with certificates, uncertainties and dates. Traceability does not make an instrument accurate; it makes its error known and comparable.

sections.h3: Calibration, verification, adjustment, and the static procedure

blocks.text: Calibration compares the instrument output with a known input produced by a standard, and records the result. It is a measurement and a record; it need not change anything. Verification is a pass/fail check: is the reading inside the allowed limits? Adjustment is the physical turning of the zero and span trims so the output matches the ideal line. You adjust after you calibrate, then calibrate again to prove the adjustment worked.

items: Hold other inputs constant — temperature, supply voltage, mounting torque, vibration — and record them; they belong on the certificate.
Pick five to ten input values over the range, including both ends.
Apply them going up (up-scale); record the output at each point.
Apply them going down (down-scale); record again. The gap at the same input is the hysteresis.
Fit a straight line: the end-point line joining the extremes, or a least-squares line.
Read sensitivity (slope), zero offset (intercept), non-linearity (largest deviation from the line) and hysteresis.
Write the certificate: range, sensitivity, zero offset, hysteresis, uncertainty, conditions held, standard used and its traceability, date.

blocks.text: Full scale in this chapter means the full-scale output, the output at the upper range limit (4.00 V in the example). It is the %FS denominator. Some texts use the span instead — here 4.00 − 0.02 = 3.98 V — which gives 0.754 % instead of 0.75 %. These static numbers are defined in Chapter 1.4; repeated-reading uncertainty is in Chapter 1.6.

spec.aria: A five-layer ladder from the SI base units at the top down through primary, secondary and working standards to the sensor being calibrated, with accuracy falling as you go down.

examples.question: A 0–200 kPa pressure sensor is calibrated against a dead-weight tester with temperature held at 25 °C and supply at 10 V. Up-scale readings: pressure 0, 50, 100, 150, 200 kPa give output 0.02, 1.01, 1.98, 3.02, 4.00 V. Find the end-point sensitivity in V/kPa and mV/kPa, the zero offset, and the largest deviation from the end-point straight line as a percentage of full scale.
steps: End-point sensitivity S = (4.00 − 0.02) V ÷ 200 kPa = 3.98 V ÷ 200 kPa = 0.0199 V/kPa = 19.9 mV/kPa.
Zero offset = output at zero input = 0.02 V.
End-point line: V(ideal) = 0.02 + 0.0199 × P, with V in volts and P in kPa.
At 0 kPa: ideal 0.020 V, measured 0.02 V, deviation 0.000 V.
At 50 kPa: ideal 1.015 V, measured 1.01 V, deviation −0.005 V.
At 100 kPa: ideal 2.010 V, measured 1.98 V, deviation −0.030 V.
At 150 kPa: ideal 3.005 V, measured 3.02 V, deviation +0.015 V.
At 200 kPa: ideal 4.000 V, measured 4.00 V, deviation 0.000 V.
As %FS using the full-scale output 4.00 V: 0.030 V ÷ 4.00 V = 0.0075 = 0.75 % FS.
examples.answer: Sensitivity 0.0199 V/kPa (19.9 mV/kPa), zero offset 0.02 V, and the largest deviation is 0.030 V = 0.75 % of the 4.00 V full-scale output.
examples.check:
P = [0, 50, 100, 150, 200]
V = [0.02, 1.01, 1.98, 3.02, 4.00]
S = (V[-1] - V[0]) / (P[-1] - P[0])
zero = V[0]
dev = [v - (zero + S * p) for p, v in zip(P, V)]
maxdev = max(abs(d) for d in dev)
print(round(S, 4))
print(round(zero, 4))
print(round(maxdev, 4))
print(round(maxdev / V[-1] * 100, 4))

traps: Never fix a span error with the zero knob, or a zero error with the span knob. Adjust zero first, then span, then recheck zero — the two interact until both settle.
An instrument that passed a verification check has not been calibrated. Verification gives pass/fail; calibration records the deviation and its uncertainty.

The denominator of %FS is the full-scale output, not the reading. A 0.03 V deviation on a 4.00 V full-scale output is 0.75 % FS but about 1.5 % of the 1.98 V reading where it occurs. Using the 3.98 V span instead gives 0.754 % FS.
Hysteresis and non-linearity are separate numbers. Hysteresis compares up-scale with down-scale at the same input; non-linearity compares one sweep with the fitted straight line.
A Celsius difference equals a kelvin difference, but absolute temperatures differ by 273.15. Mixing the two wrecks gas-law and cold-junction calculations.

quiz.q: Name the seven SI base units and give the symbol of each.
quiz.a: Metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), candela (cd).

quiz.q: State the difference between calibration and adjustment, and say which comes first.
quiz.a: Calibration compares output with a known input and records the deviation; adjustment moves the zero and span trims to reduce it. Calibrate first, adjust, then calibrate again.

quiz.q: A datasheet gives pressure sensitivity as 19.9 mV/kPa. Express it in V/psi. Take 1 psi = 6.89476 kPa.
quiz.a: 19.9 mV/kPa × 6.89476 kPa/psi = 137.2 mV/psi = 0.1372 V/psi. The kPa units cancel, leaving mV per psi.

quiz.q: Define traceability and say what it does and does not guarantee.
quiz.a: An unbroken chain of calibrations, each with a stated uncertainty and documented, ending at a primary standard. It guarantees the error is known and comparable; it does not by itself make the instrument accurate.

quiz.q: Express 1 Pa in SI base units and confirm by dimensional check that N/m² is a pressure.
quiz.a: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s², so 1 N/m² = 1 kg·m·s⁻²·m⁻² = 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². Force per area, so it is a pressure, and 1 Pa = 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻².

quiz.q: A sensor repeats its readings to within 0.1 % but its calibration certificate expired three years ago. What may and may not be claimed about its accuracy?
quiz.a: Repeatability (precision) of 0.1 % may be claimed because it was measured now. Accuracy may not: the link to a primary standard has lapsed, so there is no valid uncertainty and no proof the error has not drifted. Traceability is a claim with a date.

quiz.q: Why must temperature, supply voltage and mounting torque be held constant during calibration, and why must their values appear on the certificate?
quiz.a: They are influencing inputs; the output responds to them as well as to the measurand, so varying them folds their effect into the recorded deviation. Holding them constant makes the calibration valid only at those conditions, so the certificate must state them; otherwise a later field deviation cannot be blamed on sensor or environment.

beyond: Not for the exam. Since 2019 the SI units are fixed by constants of nature; national institutes realise the volt with Josephson junction arrays and resistance with the quantum Hall effect. Digital calibration certificates are replacing paper ones, and smart sensors keep coefficients and calibration date in memory, so the chain travels inside the device. In audited industry, an out-of-tolerance calibration forces review of every product measured since the last good one.
